To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the brain systems underlying moral sensitivity overlap with those underlying agency, intentionality, and the default mode of brain function, with additional activation in specific components for specific classes of moral emotions.
the neural substrates of moral emotions and of agency are partially shared and that this shared network is related to the default mode of brain activity.
the human brain is inherently capable of understanding the world in moral terms, endowing most people with an intuitive sense for what is fair and just, and what is wrong.
In summary, our research is concerned with

how the human brain represents and evaluates social behavior, and the implications of this research for understanding the neural bases of moral cognition and behavior, with particular relevance for social and clinical psychology.
the neural basis of moral cognition and behavior, with particular emphasis on the neural mechanisms underlying the ability to attribute agency to others, which is a key aspect of social cognition.
the neural bases of the human capacity to act in a moral way, i.e., as a moral agent.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
agency is a necessary but not sufficient condition of moral sensitivity.
the brain is inherently able, but not necessarily willing, to understand the world as moral.
agency and moral cognition are closely linked in the human brain, but that the specific neural substrates involved depend upon the type of moral emotion that is being processed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
agency, intentionality, and morality are linked in the human brain, in a manner which depends on the specific emotional valence of the moral experience.
agency and moral emotions are both associated with the activation of a common neural network.
the brain networks underlying agency, morality, and moral emotions share a number of common components, and that the specific contribution of each component depends on the type of moral emotion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the self as a moral entity is grounded in the same neural substrates that underlie the experience of self as agent.
the self as a moral being is an active participant in social interactions, which are shaped by the moral emotions that the self experiences and expresses.
agency is a key component of moral behavior, and that moral emotions and agency are both rooted in the same neural network.
